clinicalPearls: Chronic orchialgia is intermittent or constant testicular pain lasting three months or more that interferes with daily activity and for which no acute cause is found
It is frequently non-infective and, in a large proportion of men, no clear structural cause is identified, so it is often idiopathic
A thorough examination is needed to localise the pain and to exclude a testicular mass, varicocele, epididymal pathology, and hernia
Referred pain must be considered, as ureteric calculi, inguinal hernia, hip pathology, and nerve entrapment can all present as scrotal pain
Scrotal ultrasound is commonly performed largely to reassure and to exclude significant pathology rather than because it usually reveals the cause
Initial management is conservative, with reassurance, supportive underwear, analgesia, anti-inflammatory measures, and treatment of any identifiable contributor
Neuropathic pain agents and pain-clinic input help selected men, and spermatic cord blocks can be both diagnostic and therapeutic
Surgery, including microsurgical denervation of the spermatic cord or orchidectomy, is reserved for carefully selected refractory cases after detailed counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic orchialgia represents a persistent scrotal pain state that in many men cannot be attributed to a single structural lesion. Recognised contributors include previous inflammation or infection, varicocele, spermatocele, prior scrotal or inguinal surgery, and vasectomy, but a substantial proportion is idiopathic. The prevailing understanding is of a neuropathic and centrally sensitised pain process, in which the afferent nerves travelling in the spermatic cord become hypersensitive and pain is amplified within the nervous system, sometimes long after any initial insult has resolved. Referred pain, in which pathology in the ureter, hernia, hip, or lumbar nerves is perceived in the testis owing to shared innervation, is an important and treatable mechanism. Psychological factors and coexisting chronic pelvic pain frequently modulate the experience of pain.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic epididymitis and post-vasectomy pain syndrome
Referred pain from ureteric calculus or inguinal hernia
Nerve entrapment following inguinal or scrotal surgery
Musculoskeletal or hip pathology referring to the scrotum
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history and examination to localise pain and identify referred sources
Scrotal ultrasound to exclude a mass, varicocele, or epididymal lesion
Urine analysis and culture to exclude urinary infection
Sexually transmitted infection screening where relevant
Abdominal, inguinal, and musculoskeletal assessment for referred causes
Diagnostic spermatic cord block to confirm a peripheral pain source
Cross-sectional imaging where a referred or retroperitoneal cause is suspected
redFlags: A discrete or hard testicular mass on examination or imaging
Sudden severe pain with swelling raising the possibility of torsion
Systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy
Associated haematuria or flank pain suggesting a urological cause requiring investigation
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but often chronic and difficult to eradicate; many men gain adequate relief with conservative and pain-directed measures, while a smaller group with intractable pain may consider surgery, which offers benefit in selected cases but carries no guarantee of cure.
pitfalls: Attributing all scrotal pain to infection and giving repeated unnecessary antibiotics
Missing a testicular tumour presenting as chronic pain
Failing to consider and treat a referred cause such as a ureteric stone or hernia
Proceeding to orchidectomy without exhausting conservative options and counselling about persistent pain
Neglecting the neuropathic and psychological components amenable to pain-clinic input
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on chronic pelvic pain
British Association of Urological Surgeons guidance on scrotal pain
management: Conservative first-line care with reassurance, scrotal support and simple analgesia including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Identification and treatment of any specific contributor such as varicocele, epididymal pathology or an infective cause
Exclusion and treatment of referred sources (ureteric calculi, inguinal hernia, hip pathology or nerve entrapment) presenting as scrotal pain
Neuropathic pain agents such as tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentinoids for the centrally sensitised component
Diagnostic spermatic cord block to confirm a peripheral pain source, alongside pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychological support
Microsurgical spermatic cord denervation in refractory cases, with epididymectomy or orchidectomy reserved as a last resort
Multidisciplinary chronic pain and andrology referral for intractable pain
